questions.stem: A 58 year old man has 3 weeks of neck pain with aching along the medial border of his right scapula. He struggles to lift his right arm sideways and to rotate it outwards. There is reduced sensation over the outer upper arm and the supinator reflex is absent. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which nerve root is most likely affected?
questions.e: C5 radiculopathy causes medial scapular pain, weak deltoid/supraspinatus/infraspinatus, lateral upper arm sensory loss and a lost supinator reflex.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve root is most likely affected?

clues: medial border of his right scapula
steps.x: Weak abduction and external rotation (deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus) with lateral upper arm numbness.

elim: C6 causes pain into the thumb and index finger with a depressed brachioradialis reflex.
C7 weakens triceps and depresses the triceps reflex.
C8 causes sensory loss over the little finger.
T1 causes ulnar forearm sensory loss and weak finger abduction.

steps.x: Answer A: C5. Weak shoulder abduction + lateral upper arm numbness = C5.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has 2 weeks of neck pain that shoots down the outer side of her left arm into her thumb and index finger, worse on turning her head to the left. She has mild weakness of elbow flexion. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: C6 radiculopathy gives pain down the lateral arm into the index finger with a depressed brachioradialis reflex (it also contributes to the biceps reflex).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination?

clues: into her thumb and index finger
steps.x: Pain to thumb and index finger is a C6 dermatome; its reflex is brachioradialis.

elim: The ankle reflex is S1.
The triceps reflex is C7.
The knee reflex is L3/L4.
Finger abduction is T1.

steps.x: Answer B: Depressed brachioradialis reflex. C6: thumb/index finger pain, depressed brachioradialis reflex.

questions.stem: A 52 year old builder has 3 weeks of neck pain with pain at the inner edge of his right shoulder blade, spreading down the back of his arm to his middle finger. He finds it hard to push open heavy doors and to flex his wrist against resistance. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 132/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: C7 radiculopathy causes medial scapular pain, weak triceps and wrist flexors and a depressed triceps reflex.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination?

clues: inner edge of his right shoulder blade
steps.x: Weak triceps (pushing) and wrist flexion with middle finger pain is C7.

elim: The knee reflex is L3/L4.
The biceps reflex is C5/C6.
Phalen's is a median nerve test for carpal tunnel syndrome.
Thenar wasting is a median nerve sign.

steps.x: Answer C: Depressed triceps reflex. C7: weak triceps/wrist flexors, depressed triceps reflex.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has 1 month of neck pain radiating down the inside of her left arm, worse when she extends and turns her neck to the left. She has numbness over her left little finger only. She does not lean on her elbows. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which nerve root is most likely affected?
questions.e: C8 radiculopathy causes sensory loss over the 5th finger; neck pain provoked by neck movement points to a root rather than the ulnar nerve.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve root is most likely affected?

clues: neck pain radiating down the inside of her left arm
worse when she extends and turns her neck
numbness over her left little finger
steps.x: Neck-provoked arm pain with little finger numbness localises to the C8 root.

elim: C5 causes lateral upper arm numbness and weak deltoid.
C6 causes thumb and index finger symptoms.
L5 is a lumbar root supplying the leg.
T2 supplies the axilla and upper chest, not the hand.

steps.x: Answer C: C8. Little finger numbness with radiating neck pain = C8.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has 3 weeks of pain in his left hip and front of his thigh. He finds it hard to lift his left leg to climb into his car. Hip flexion and knee extension are weak and there is reduced sensation over the front and inner thigh. The knee jerk is reduced but the ankle jerk is normal.
questions.q: Which nerve root is most likely affected?
questions.e: L3 radiculopathy causes hip/thigh pain, weak hip flexion and knee extension, sensory loss over the anterior/medial thigh and a reduced knee jerk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve root is most likely affected?

clues: Hip flexion and knee extension are weak
steps.x: Weak hip flexion with anterior/medial thigh numbness and reduced knee jerk is L3.

elim: L5 causes foot drop and dorsum of foot numbness with normal reflexes.
S1 reduces the ankle reflex and weakens plantar flexion.
S2 supplies the posterior thigh and does not cause weak hip flexion.
T12 supplies the lower abdomen and groin, not thigh muscles.

steps.x: Answer A: L3. L3: weak hip flexion, anterior/medial thigh numbness, reduced knee jerk.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has 2 weeks of low back pain radiating over the front of her right knee to the inner side of her lower leg and ankle. Knee extension is weak and the right patellar reflex is absent. There is reduced sensation over the medial malleolus. Ankle dorsiflexion and plantar flexion are normal.
questions.q: Which nerve root is most likely affected?
questions.e: L4 radiculopathy gives an absent knee reflex, weak knee extension and sensory change around the knee, medial lower leg and malleolus.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve root is most likely affected?

clues: inner side of her lower leg and ankle
steps.x: Absent knee jerk with medial lower leg numbness to the malleolus is the L4 pattern.

elim: L2 supplies the upper anterior thigh and hip flexors.
L5 causes foot drop with dorsum of foot numbness.
S1 causes a reduced ankle reflex and lateral foot numbness.
S2 supplies the posterior thigh.

steps.x: Answer B: L4. L4: absent knee jerk, medial leg and malleolus sensory change.

questions.stem: A 41 year old warehouse worker has 10 days of back pain radiating down the outer side of his left calf to the top of his foot after lifting a box. His left foot slaps the floor as he walks. Straight leg raise is positive at 40°. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot
Sensory loss over the sole of the foot
questions.e: L5 radiculopathy gives foot drop, slapping gait, weak hip abduction and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot, with reflexes usually normal.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination?

clues: outer side of his left calf to the top of his foot
steps.x: Lateral calf to dorsum of foot pain with foot drop = L5, which supplies the dorsum of the foot.

elim: An absent ankle reflex is an S1 sign; L5 reflexes are usually normal.
The knee reflex is L4.
The sole is S1 and tibial nerve territory.
Weak plantar flexion is S1.

steps.x: Answer C: Sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. L5: foot drop and dorsum of foot numbness; reflexes normal.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has 1 week of pain from his right buttock down the back of his leg to the outer edge of his foot, after moving furniture. He cannot stand on tiptoe on his right leg. Straight leg raise is positive at 30°. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: S1 radiculopathy causes posterolateral leg pain, weak plantar flexion, sensory loss over the lateral foot, a positive sciatic stretch test and a reduced ankle reflex.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
Weak plantar flexion with lateral foot pain is S1, whose reflex is the ankle jerk.

elim: The knee reflex is L3/L4.
An upgoing plantar is an upper motor neuron sign.
The triceps reflex is C7.
Dorsiflexion is L4/L5.

steps.x: Answer C: Reduced right ankle reflex. S1: weak plantar flexion, lateral foot numbness, reduced ankle reflex.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has 5 days of severe pain from her lower back radiating down the back of her right thigh and calf, which started while lifting her suitcase. Pain is worse when she coughs. Straight leg raise reproduces the leg pain. She has no bladder or bowel symptoms and no saddle numbness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her leg pain?
questions.e: Lumbar radiculopathy is most importantly caused by disc prolapse, giving back pain radiating down the leg (sciatica).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her leg pain?

clues: Straight leg raise reproduces the leg pain
steps.x: Acute lifting injury, dermatomal leg pain worse on coughing and a positive straight leg raise.

elim: This causes inflammatory back pain with morning stiffness in young adults, not acute radiating leg pain.
This causes buttock pain without a positive straight leg raise from a disc.
There are no red flags such as age, weight loss or cancer history.
This causes localised back pain, typically in older osteoporotic patients.

steps.x: Answer B: Lumbar disc prolapse. Sciatica after lifting = lumbar disc prolapse.

questions.stem: A 66 year old retired plumber has 2 months of neck pain and pain radiating down his right arm into his thumb, with weak elbow flexion and a reduced brachioradialis reflex. He has had neck stiffness for years. A previous X-ray showed disc space narrowing at several cervical levels. He has no history of trauma.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Cervical radiculopathy is usually due to disc herniation or degeneration, giving neck and arm pain in a dermatomal pattern.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause?

clues: disc space narrowing at several cervical levels
radiating down his right arm into his thumb
steps.x: Older patient, chronic neck stiffness and degenerative changes with a C6 root pattern.

elim: Brachial neuritis causes acute severe shoulder pain followed by weakness, not chronic neck pain.
Carpal tunnel does not cause neck pain or a reduced reflex.
MS causes upper motor neuron signs, not a single root pattern with neck pain.
An apical tumour affects lower roots (C8/T1) with Horner's syndrome.

steps.x: Answer C: Degenerative cervical disc disease. Cervical radiculopathy is usually degenerative disc disease.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with 3 weeks of sciatica now has numbness around his anus and genitals and bilateral leg weakness. He has not passed urine since last night. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Both ankle reflexes are absent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
questions.e: Cauda equina syndrome causes saddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone, urinary retention, bilateral weakness, reduced tone and areflexia.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?

clues: numbness around his anus and genitals
steps.x: Saddle anaesthesia, retention and bilateral areflexia = cauda equina syndrome.

elim: Cauda equina is a lower motor neuron lesion, so reflexes are reduced or absent.
Extensor plantars indicate an upper motor neuron (cord) lesion.
Tone is reduced in cauda equina syndrome.
A sensory level indicates a thoracic cord lesion.

steps.x: Answer D: Reduced anal sphincter tone. Cauda equina: saddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone, retention.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has 4 weeks of low back pain with pain down both legs. Today she noticed difficulty starting to pass urine. A bladder scan shows 850 mL. She reports no numbness yet. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. Ankle reflexes are reduced bilaterally.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Back pain plus urinary retention is cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise, even before saddle anaesthesia develops.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Back pain with bilateral leg symptoms and retention is a red flag.

elim: There is no fever or dysuria, and retention with bilateral leg pain and reduced reflexes is neurological.
Bilateral symptoms with urinary retention must be treated as cauda equina.
Mechanical back pain does not cause retention or reflex loss.
A thoracic cord lesion causes upper motor neuron signs and a sensory level.

steps.x: Answer C: Cauda equina syndrome. Back pain + urinary retention = treat as cauda equina.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has 3 weeks of back pain radiating down the outer side of his right calf to the dorsum of his foot. He has foot drop, and both ankle inversion and eversion are weak. Hip abduction is weak. Knee and ankle reflexes are normal. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: L5 radiculopathy gives foot drop with weak inversion as well as eversion and weak hip abduction; pain runs from the lateral calf to the dorsum of the foot.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: back pain radiating down the outer side of his right calf
both ankle inversion and eversion are weak
steps.x: Weak inversion and hip abduction place the lesion at the root, not the peroneal nerve.

elim: Common peroneal palsy spares inversion and hip abduction and has no back pain.
Deep peroneal palsy spares eversion and only affects the first web space.
MND has no pain or sensory loss and mixes upper and lower motor neuron signs.
S1 reduces the ankle reflex and weakens plantar flexion.

steps.x: Answer C: L5 radiculopathy. Foot drop + weak inversion + weak hip abduction = L5 root.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has 6 weeks of neck pain radiating to the inner side of her right forearm. She has numbness along the ulnar edge of the forearm and weakness when spreading her fingers. Grip is otherwise normal and there is no ptosis. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 126/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which nerve root is most likely affected?
questions.e: T1 radiculopathy causes pain and sensory loss along the ulnar forearm edge with weakness of finger abduction.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve root is most likely affected?
Medial forearm sensory loss and weak finger abduction (interossei) = T1.

elim: C5 weakens deltoid and causes lateral upper arm numbness.
C6 causes thumb and index finger symptoms.
C7 weakens triceps with middle finger symptoms.
L4 is a lumbar root.

steps.x: Answer E: T1. T1: ulnar forearm sensory loss and weak finger abduction.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has 10 weeks of right C6 radicular arm pain and numbness of her thumb despite analgesia and physiotherapy. Elbow flexion is now weaker. She is referred to a spinal surgeon, who wants to see the nerve root compression before considering surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Nerve conduction studies of the median nerve
Plain X-ray of the cervical spine
questions.e: MRI of the spine is the gold-standard imaging for radiculopathy, showing nerve root compression.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

clues: wants to see the nerve root compression
steps.x: Soft tissue (disc and nerve root) is best shown by MRI.

elim: The brain is not the site of a root lesion.
These assess carpal tunnel, not root compression.
X-ray shows bone but not root compression and has limited use.
This assesses rotator cuff disease.

steps.x: Answer B: MRI cervical spine. Gold standard for radiculopathy = MRI spine.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man has 1 week of left sciatica after playing squash. Straight leg raise is positive. Power, reflexes and sensation are normal and he has no bladder, bowel or saddle symptoms. He asks for an X-ray of his back to see what is wrong. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 72 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Initial diagnosis of radiculopathy is clinical from history and examination; no imaging is needed initially and X-ray has limited use.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: no bladder, bowel or saddle symptoms
steps.x: Uncomplicated acute sciatica with no red flags is a clinical diagnosis.

elim: CT adds radiation and does not change management in uncomplicated sciatica.
There are no red flags for cauda equina.
X-ray has limited use and does not show the disc or nerve root.
These are not needed for a clinical radiculopathy.

steps.x: Answer E: No imaging: diagnosis is clinical. Acute sciatica: clinical diagnosis, no imaging initially; X-ray unhelpful.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has 2 weeks of neck pain radiating to his right shoulder with aching at the medial scapular border. Deltoid and supraspinatus are weak and he has numbness over the outer upper arm. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg. A student examines his reflexes.
questions.q: Which reflex is most likely to be reduced?
questions.e: The biceps and supinator reflexes test C4/C5 (with C6), so they are reduced in a C5 radiculopathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which reflex is most likely to be reduced?

clues: numbness over the outer upper arm
steps.x: Weak deltoid and supraspinatus with lateral upper arm numbness is C5; its reflex is biceps/supinator.

elim: The ankle reflex tests S1.
Finger flexion tests C8.
The knee reflex tests L3/L4.
The triceps reflex tests C7.

steps.x: Answer B: Biceps reflex. C5: reduced biceps/supinator reflex.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman with 2 weeks of sciatica has developed numbness of her buttocks and inner thighs and bilateral leg weakness since yesterday. She has urinary retention with 700 mL on bladder scan. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine
questions.e: Suspected cauda equina syndrome needs emergency MRI, the gold standard for showing root compression, with urgent surgical referral.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: numbness of her buttocks and inner thighs
steps.x: Saddle anaesthesia, bilateral weakness and retention = suspected cauda equina: image now.

elim: This does not show the cauda equina roots well and is not the right test.
X-ray cannot show root compression.
These delay diagnosis of a surgical emergency.
Cauda equina needs emergency imaging, not routine.

steps.x: Answer B: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine. Suspected cauda equina: emergency MRI.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has 1 week of right sciatica after gardening. There is no weakness or sensory loss and no bladder, bowel or saddle symptoms. She has started ibuprofen and been referred to physiotherapy. She is worried she will need an operation and asks how likely the pain is to settle.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: About 90% settle within 3 months without surgery
Most need a steroid injection to settle
Surgery is needed if it lasts more than a week
questions.e: Around 90% of sciatica settles within 3 months with conservative management and rarely needs specialist referral.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice?

clues: no bladder, bowel or saddle symptoms
how likely the pain is to settle
steps.x: Uncomplicated sciatica has a good natural history.

elim: This reverses the true natural history.
Sciatica usually takes weeks, not days.
Injections are for persistent symptoms only.
Referral is considered only after 4 to 6 weeks without improvement.

steps.x: Answer B: About 90% settle within 3 months without surgery. Sciatica: 90% resolve within 3 months conservatively.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has 10 days of neck pain radiating down his left arm to his middle finger. Power is full and reflexes are normal. He has no history of cancer, fever or weight loss and no gait disturbance. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Paracetamol or an NSAID with physiotherapy
questions.e: The standard first-line approach to radiculopathy is analgesia (paracetamol, NSAIDs) plus physiotherapy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

clues: Power is full and reflexes are normal
no history of cancer, fever or weight loss
steps.x: Uncomplicated radicular pain without red flags: conservative first.

elim: Prolonged immobilisation is not recommended.
There are no red flags or progressive deficit.
Steroids are not first-line for radiculopathy.
Surgery is for persistent pain or progressive deficit.

steps.x: Answer D: Paracetamol or an NSAID with physiotherapy. First line: analgesia plus physiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has 4 weeks of left sciatica with burning, shooting pain down to her foot despite naproxen and physiotherapy. She has no weakness or bladder symptoms. She has a history of closed-angle glaucoma treated by her ophthalmologist. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to add for her pain?
questions.e: Neuropathic radicular pain is treated with amitriptyline or gabapentin; amitriptyline's anticholinergic effects make gabapentin the safer choice here.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate drug to add for her pain?
Neuropathic pain needs amitriptyline or gabapentin; glaucoma rules out amitriptyline.

elim: Amitriptyline is anticholinergic and can precipitate closed-angle glaucoma and urinary retention.
Weak opioids do not target neuropathic pain well.
Benzodiazepines are not recommended for sciatica.
Oral steroids are not a neuropathic agent.

steps.x: Answer C: Gabapentin. Neuropathic radicular pain: amitriptyline or gabapentin.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has 3 months of right L5 radicular pain. He has had NSAIDs, physiotherapy and gabapentin with only partial relief. Power and reflexes are normal and there are no red flags. MRI shows a small L4/L5 disc protrusion contacting the right L5 root. He would prefer to avoid an operation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Persistent symptoms despite conservative management can be treated with a steroid injection.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
Conservative and neuropathic treatment have only partly worked, and he wants to avoid surgery.

elim: Bed rest is not recommended and delays recovery.
There is no cauda equina or acute deficit.
IVIG is for Guillain-Barré syndrome.
He has persistent symptoms that need further treatment.

steps.x: Answer C: Epidural steroid injection. Persistent radicular pain despite conservative care: steroid injection.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman has 3 weeks of left L5 radiculopathy. Over the past week her foot drop has worsened from mild to severe (dorsiflexion now 1/5) and she trips repeatedly. She has no saddle anaesthesia and normal bladder function. MRI shows a large L4/L5 disc prolapse compressing the left L5 root.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Continue physiotherapy and review in 3 months
Referral to spinal surgery for decompression
questions.e: Surgery is indicated for a severe or progressive neurological deficit as well as for pain that does not settle.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
A progressing motor deficit is an indication for surgery.

elim: A severe and progressive deficit should not wait.
Injections treat pain, not a progressive motor deficit.
Neuropathic drugs treat pain, not weakness.
IVIG is for Guillain-Barré syndrome.

steps.x: Answer E: Referral to spinal surgery for decompression. Severe or progressive deficit = surgical referral.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man phones his GP with 2 days of bilateral sciatica and new numbness when he wipes after opening his bowels. He has some difficulty starting to pass urine. He is otherwise well. He has a history of a previous L5/S1 disc prolapse.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate action?
o: Book a routine GP appointment next week
Immediate referral to hospital for emergency assessment
Prescribe amitriptyline and review in 2 weeks
questions.e: Suspected cauda equina syndrome (bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, bladder symptoms) needs urgent emergency referral.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate action?
Saddle numbness plus bladder symptoms with sciatica = suspected cauda equina.

elim: Suspected cauda equina is a surgical emergency.
Delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.
This misses an emergency.
A routine referral is far too slow.

steps.x: Answer B: Immediate referral to hospital for emergency assessment. Suspected cauda equina: emergency referral the same day.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has had right S1 sciatica for 2 weeks. She is taking ibuprofen and has started physiotherapy, and her pain is slowly improving. Power and reflexes are normal and she has no red flags. She asks when she should be referred to a spinal surgeon.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue conservative treatment; refer if not settling after 4 to 6 weeks
questions.e: Sciatica is treated with NSAIDs and physiotherapy first; routine referral to spinal surgery is for pain not settling after 4 to 6 weeks.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Only 2 weeks in and improving: keep going; the step-up point is 4 to 6 weeks.

elim: There are no red flags.
She is improving and it is too early.
Routine referral is considered after 4 to 6 weeks of failed treatment.
Physiotherapy is part of first-line treatment.

steps.x: Answer A: Continue conservative treatment; refer if not settling after 4 to 6 weeks. Refer for surgery if not settling after 4 to 6 weeks.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has left S1 radiculopathy from a disc prolapse. He has pain in a strip down the back of his leg to the outer foot, weak plantar flexion and a reduced ankle reflex. A student asks why one compressed root gives such a precise pattern.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Each muscle is supplied by a single peripheral nerve
Each root supplies a specific dermatome, myotome and reflex arc
Pain is referred from the disc itself
The spinal cord is compressed at the level of the disc
Upper motor neuron damage spreads distally
questions.e: Each nerve root supplies a particular dermatome, myotome and reflex arc, so the deficit pattern localises the level.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation?

clues: pain in a strip down the back of his leg
steps.x: Dermatome (sensory strip), myotome (plantar flexion) and reflex (ankle) all belong to S1.

elim: Many muscles receive several roots; the pattern reflects the root, not one nerve.
Disc pain is non-dermatomal back pain, not a precise limb pattern.
The cord ends at L1/L2, so a lumbar disc compresses a root, not the cord.
Root lesions are lower motor neuron lesions.

steps.x: Answer B: Each root supplies a specific dermatome, myotome and reflex arc. Root pattern localises the level: dermatome, myotome, reflex.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has back pain and right leg pain after lifting. MRI shows a right posterolateral disc prolapse at the L5/S1 level. A student asks which nerve root is most likely to be compressed.
questions.q: Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
questions.e: A posterolateral disc usually compresses the root exiting below the disc space, so an L5/S1 disc affects S1.

steps.x: The question asks: Which nerve root is most likely compressed?

clues: right posterolateral disc prolapse at the L5/S1 level
steps.x: Posterolateral discs catch the traversing root, numbered after the lower vertebra.

elim: L3 exits well above this level.
L4 exits at L4/L5 foramen above the disc.
L5 is affected by an L4/L5 posterolateral disc.
S2 exits lower and is not usually compressed by an L5/S1 posterolateral disc.

steps.x: Answer D: S1. Posterolateral disc compresses the root below: L5/S1 disc = S1.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has a massive central L4/L5 disc prolapse. He has bilateral leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention, rather than pain in one leg. MRI shows the spinal cord ends at L1/L2 and is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his bilateral and sphincter symptoms?
o: Compression of a single L5 root
Compression of multiple lumbosacral roots below the end of the spinal cord
Compression of the conus at T12
questions.e: The cauda equina is the bundle of lumbosacral roots below the cord terminus (L1/L2); compressing it causes bilateral leg, bladder, bowel and saddle disturbance.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for his bilateral and sphincter symptoms?
Below L1/L2 there is no cord, only the bundle of roots; a central disc compresses many of them.

elim: A single root lesion causes unilateral symptoms without sphincter loss.
MRI shows the cord and conus are normal.
This is Guillain-Barré, not a disc lesion.
There is no spinal cord at L4.

steps.x: Answer B: Compression of multiple lumbosacral roots below the end of the spinal cord. Cauda equina = many lumbosacral roots below the cord terminus.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has cauda equina syndrome from a central L5/S1 disc prolapse confirmed on MRI. She has saddle anaesthesia and painless urinary retention. The on-call spinal surgeon plans surgery tonight. A student asks why it cannot wait until the next routine list.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason for urgent surgery?
o: The disc will calcify and cannot be removed later
The leg pain will become untreatable
There is a risk of meningitis
Urgent decompression prevents permanent bladder, bowel and saddle damage
questions.e: Cauda equina syndrome is a true surgical emergency: urgent decompression prevents permanent damage to bladder, bowel and saddle function.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely reason for urgent surgery?

clues: saddle anaesthesia and painless urinary retention
steps.x: Root compression that persists leads to irreversible sphincter loss.

elim: This is not the reason for urgency.
Discs do not calcify within days.
The urgency is about permanent loss of sphincter and saddle function, not pain.
Disc prolapse does not cause infection.

steps.x: Answer E: Urgent decompression prevents permanent bladder, bowel and saddle damage. Cauda equina: urgent decompression to prevent permanent damage.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has left C7 radicular pain. CT shows large osteophytes narrowing the left C6/C7 intervertebral foramen but no disc herniation. A student asks how the osteophytes cause his arm pain.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
